abstract: In protein biophysics, the separation between the functionally important residues (forming the active site or binding surface) and those that create the overall structure (the fold) is a well-established and fundamental concept. Identifying and modifying those functional sites is critical for protein engineering but computationally non-trivial, and requires significant domain knowledge. To automate this process from a data-driven perspective, we propose a disentangled Wasserstein autoencoder with an auxiliary classifier, which isolates the function-related patterns from the rest with theoretical guarantees. This enables one-pass protein sequence editing and improves the understanding of the resulting sequences and editing actions involved. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we apply it to T-cell receptors (TCRs), a well-studied structure-function case. We show that our method can be used to alter the function of TCRs without changing the structural backbone, outperforming several competing methods in generation quality and efficiency, and requiring only 10\% of the running time needed by baseline models. To our knowledge, this is the first approach that utilizes disentangled representations for TCR engineering.

# Learning Disentangled Representations for T Cell Receptor Design Martin Renqiang Min $^{1*†}$ , Tianxiao Li $^{1,2†}$ , Hongyu Guo $^{3,4}$ , Filippo Grazioli $^{5}$ and Mark Gerstein $^{2,6,7,8}$ $^{1}$ NEC Labs America, 4 Independence Way, Princeton, 08540, New Jersey, USA. $^{2}$ Program in Computational Biology & Bioinformatics, Yale University, New Haven, 06520, Connecticut, USA. $^{3}$ National Research Council Canada, 1200 Montreal Road, Ottawa, K1A 0R6, Ontario, Canada. $^{4}$ School of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, University of Ottawa, 800 King Edward Ave, Ottawa, K1N 6N5, Ontario, Canada. $^{5}$ NEC Labs Europe, Kurfürsten-Anlage 36, Heidelberg, 69115, Germany. $^{6}$ Department of Molecular Biophysics and Biochemistry, Yale University, New Haven, 06520, Connecticut, USA. $^{7}$ Department of Computer Science, Yale University, New Haven, 06520, Connecticut, USA. $^{8}$ Department of Statistics & Data Science, Yale University, New Haven, 06520, Connecticut, USA. *Corresponding author(s). E-mail(s): renqiang@nec-labs.com; Contributing authors: tianxiao.li@yale.edu; hongyu.guo@uottawa.ca; filippo.grazioli@neclab.eu; mark@gersteinlab.org; †These authors contributed equally to this work. # Abstract The interaction between T cell receptors (TCRs) and peptide antigens is critical for human immune responses. Designing antigen-specific TCRs, therefore, represents an important step in adoptive immunotherapy. As experimental procedures for TCR engineering are expensive, leveraging machine learning methods to learn and optimize informative TCR representations to computationally generate antigen-specific candidate TCRs has recently attracted a surge of interest. In particular, learning representations that isolate salient (or explanatory) factors to explicitly capture the interplay between TCR and antigen is crucial for model explainability, training sample efficiency, and effective conditional TCR modification, and thus is highly demanding. In this paper, we propose a novel strategy to attain such goal. Our proposed autoencoder model, coined TCR-dAE, aims at generating disentangled embeddings where different sets of dimensions correspond to generic TCR sequence backbones and antigen binding-related patterns, respectively. As a result, the disentangled embedding space formed not only improves interpretability of the model but also enables one-pass optimization of TCR sequences conditioned on antigen binding properties. By modifying the binding-related parts of the embedding, TCR-dAE generates TCR sequences with enhanced binding affinity while maintaining the backbone of the template TCR. It outperforms several baseline methods by generating larger amounts of valid TCR sequences with higher binding affinity to the given antigen. Promisingly, the functional embeddings constructed by TCR-dAE can also be used as a signature for distinguishing the peptide-binding property of TCR sequences, which can further benefit applications such as classification and clustering of TCR specificity. # 1 Introduction T cells play an important role in the adaptive immune response [1]. Activation of T cells happen when T cell receptors (TCRs) recognize and bind to peptide antigens presented by the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) of antigen presenting cells [2]. Human beings have a large repertoire of TCR variants as a result of gene recombination [3], allowing responses to a wide variety of antigens from viral-infected cells, tumor cells, etc.. The high variability of TCRs gives rise to adoptive immunotherapy, where T cells with specifically designed TCRs, which target certain tumor peptide antigens more effectively, are provided to the patient [4]. As experimental methods are time-consuming and expensive, it is desirable to computationally prioritize candidate TCRs with potentially enhanced binding affinity to the peptide of interest. Most human TCRs are heterodimers comprised of a $\mathrm{TCR}\alpha$ chain and a $\mathrm{TCR}\beta$ chain [2]. Each chain contains three complementarity-determining regions (CDRs), CDR1, 2 and 3, which are highly variable due to gene recombination. It has been generally believed that the CDR3 region of the $\beta$ chain is mainly responsible for antigen recognition [5]. Thus, most computational methods focus on the $\mathrm{CDR}3\beta$ region for modelling the antigen recognition of TCRs, and we will be using “CDR3β” and “TCR” interchangeably, unless otherwise specified. Traditional methods for designing novel biological sequences with desired properties require significant domain knowledge, and are usually limited to specific cases. Several recent studies make use of deep generative models [6] or reinforcement learning [7] to learn from large-scale data the implicit functional features and how to optimize these features, using black-box optimization techniques, to introduce desired TCR functions and properties. Here we approach the TCR optimization task with explicit functional features, in a similar fashion as a style transfer problem in natural language processing, where the "style" (e.g. writing style, tone or sentiment) of a sentence is modified while the "content", namely the general meaning, is maintained [8]. The key of such disentangled representation learning (DRL) technique is to map the input data into an embedding space where certain dimensions correspond to specific properties of the data. Through isolating salient (or explanatory) factors of variation in the data, learning disentangled representations will not only make the embedding space more interpretable, but also enables effective conditioned generation where some properties are modified while others are maintained through manipulating certain embedding dimensions. Such characteristics of the DRL technique potentially offer an effective solution to the TCR optimization task for the following reasons. First, to optimize a TCR, it is desirable to only modify a limited number of sites to enhance the binding affinity, while preserving the sequence backbone so that the optimized sequence is still a valid TCR. Second, different from existing methods where mutations are often iteratively introduced to the sequence, a DRL model requires only one pass to generate optimized sequences. Finally, the functional embedding, separated from the sequence backbone, can be used as a novel discriminative feature for the binding affinity of the TCR, which would facilitate model interpretation and large-scale conditioned generation and optimization. Nevertheless, learning disentangled representations for TCR is not trivial owing to the extremely complex interactions between TCRs and antigens. To attain the aforementioned goal, we devise a disentangled autoencoder that embeds the TCR sequence into a "functional" embedding and a "structural" embedding, where the former encodes patterns that are responsible for peptide recognition and the latter contains information about the generic structural context. This is achieved by two auxiliary losses, which ensure that the functional embedding encodes the functional information while being independent from the structural embedding. We demonstrate that, through modifying only the functional embedding isolated for known non-binding TCRs given the peptide to generate new binding TCRs, our model outperforms several baselines, including random mutation-based methods and Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS), in generating 10 times more valid TCR sequences with high binding affinity in much shorter running time. To our knowledge, ours is the first study that leverages disentangled representation for TCR sequence optimization, and could potentially be generalized to other protein functions. # 2 Related Works # TCR-peptide binding prediction A large amount of literature investigates the prediction of the interaction between TCRs and peptides. Early methods use consensus motifs or simple structural patterns like k-mers as predictive features [9-12]. Other methods assess the binding energy for the TCR-peptide pair using physical or structural modelling [13, 14]. In recent years, several deep neural network architectures have been applied to this task [12, 15-18], using TCR and peptide sequences as input. Specifically, Weber et al. [12] use an attention-based neural network and find that the attention patterns highlight some chemically-related interaction sites. This indicates that deep learning models have the potential to capture biological-relevant patterns that are important for the binding. # Computational biological sequence design Traditional methods of computational biological sequence design uses search algorithms, where random mutations are introduced and then selected by the specified criteria [19-21]. Deep generative models like variational autoencoder (VAE) [22] or generative adversarial nework (GAN) [6] have also been successfully applied to biological sequences such as DNA. By approximating the distribution of sequences with the desired property, it is then possible to generate new sequences accordingly. Other recent approaches include learning a policy that optimize the given sequence towards a reward function using reinforcement learning (RL) frameworks [7], and iteratively picking generated sequences with the highest score to update the model [23]. For TCR generation specifically, we would need to condition on the target antigenic peptide as the desired property. # Disentangled representation learning (DRL) The formulation of DRL tasks depends on its nature, such as separating "style" and "content" of a piece of text [24] or a picture [25], or static and dynamic parts of a video [26, 27]. The disentangled representations improve interpretability of the model, and can be used for style transfer [24, 25, 28] and conditional generation [29, 30]. Several regularization methods have been used to achieve disentanglement, including adversarial loss [28, 29], mutual information constraints [24, 26], and self-supervising auxiliary tasks [26]. To our knowledge, there has been very limited attempts to apply DRL to biological sequence designs. Table 1 Statistics of the training set. Samples from NetTCR datasets are incorporated into both. # 3 Materials and methods # 3.1 Datasets Interacting TCR-peptide pairs are obtained from VDJDB [31] and MCPAS [32]. We also merge each set with experimentally-validated negative pairs from NetTCR [16] if the TCR exists in the respective datasets. As the ground-truth negative samples were scarce, we expanded the negative set to $5\mathrm{x}$ of the positive by swapping the peptide in the positive pairs with all other peptides in the dataset, and treating all unobserved pairs as negative. We then use ERGO [18], a state-of-the-art method for TCR-binding prediction, to select peptides with auroc $>0.9$ and $\mathrm{aupr} > 0.9$ . For this and all subsequent ERGO-based predictions, we use the pre-trained weights from https://github.com/ louzounlab/ERGO. Specifically, as the dataset is very imbalanced, we downsample all peptides to at most 400 positive pairs. To make sure the model captures peptide-specific information, for every TCR in the positive set, we add its unobserved pairings with other peptides to the negative set. We then split the TCRs into train/test/validation sets with a ratio of 8:1:1, and put all pairings of each TCR to the respective subset, to ensure all TCRs in the test and validation sets are not seen in the training. For each set, the positive samples are upsampled by the negative/positive ratio of the original dataset. The statistics of the resulting dataset is shown in Table 1 (see Extended Data Table 1 and 2 for more details). For each peptide, we generate an additional dataset with 5000 TCR sequences that do not overlap with the training set. This set is used for the optimization experiment (see the "TCR optimization" section for more details). The input data sample is formulated as a triplet $\{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{u},y\}$ , where $\mathbf{x}$ is the TCR sequence, $\mathbf{u}$ is the peptide, and $y$ is the binary label indicating the interaction. # 3.2 Problem formulation The problem of TCR optimization is defined as follows: given a TCR sequence and a peptide it originally could not bind to, introduce a minimal number of mutations to the TCR so that it gains the ability to bind to the given peptide. In the meantime, the modified TCR should remain a valid TCR, with no major changes in the structural backbone. We consider the patterns of a protein sequence as a higher level combination of the identities and positions of the amino acids within the protein. Based on the assumption that only certain amino acids within the TCR should be responsible for interacting with the peptide, we could define two kinds of patterns in the TCR sequence: - The "functional patterns" comprise of the amino acids that define the peptide binding property of the TCR. Altering these patterns will either make the TCR lose the current binding target, or gain a new binding target. Also, TCRs that bind to the same peptide should have similar functional patterns. - The "structural patterns" refer to all other patterns that are not related to peptide binding. As some of these patterns may be responsible for defining the structural backbone, altering them does not change the function, but would probably make the sequence no longer a valid TCR. From these definitions, we expect the two patterns to be independent from each other. Thus, we employ a disentangled representation learning framework to extract and separate these two patterns. Furthermore, optimizing a TCR towards the given peptide involves only modifying the isolated functional patterns. # 3.3 Disentangled autoencoder Here we describe our TCR-dAE framework, which learns the disentangled embeddings of the input TCR sequence that corresponds to the aforementioned two patterns. Notations used in this section can be found in Table 2. Given an input triplet $\{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{u},y\}$ , the embedding space of $\mathbf{x}$ is separated into two parts: $\mathbf{z} = \mathrm{concat}(\mathbf{z}_f,\mathbf{z}_s)$ , where $\mathbf{z}_f$ is the functional embedding related to peptide binding, and $\mathbf{z}_s$ is the structural embedding. We use two separate encoders [33] for the embeddings, respectively. $\mathbf{x}$ is provided to the encoders as an one-hot encoding of the sequence, then transformed into the continuous space by a look-up embedding layer. Both encoders contain a 1-layer transformer encoder layer with self attention, followed by a 2-layer multi-layer perceptron (MLP) which transforms the transformer encoder output into the pre-defined embedding dimensions: $$ \mathbf {z} _ {i} = \Theta_ {i} (\mathbf {x}) = \mathrm {M L P} (\mathrm {s e l f - a t t n} (\mathrm {e m b} (\mathbf {x})))) $$ where $i \in \{s, f\}$ and the two encoders share the same first embedding layer. We use self attention because it has been shown to successfully model protein sequences and capture long-range interactions between the amino acids [34, 35]. The decoder is a long short-term memory (LSTM) recurrent neural network [36], which can be effectively used for autoregressive generation. It takes the functional and structural embeddings $\mathbf{z}_f, \mathbf{z}_s$ and peptide $\mathbf{u}$ as input and reconstructs the original sequence $\mathbf{x}$ . ![](images/37586638774962574cf114912bd5c04e5d5961e81a5aac84cc3d2dd7a4b2cd2a.jpg) ![](images/e9443aba5a667ac1447e0f34843a6bdd3d1b3f273c6a8c1e934fb785304411e5.jpg) Fig. 1 (A) The disentangled autoencoder framework. (B) Method for sequence modification. $\mathbf{z}_s$ of the template sequence and a modified $\mathbf{z}_f^{\prime}$ , which represents the desired peptide binding property, are fed to the decoder to generate optimized TCRs. # 3.3.1 Functional embedding The functional embedding $\mathbf{z}_f$ is encoded by the functional encoder $\Theta_f(\mathbf{x})$ . In order to make sure $\mathbf{z}_f$ carries information about binding of the given peptide $\mathbf{u}$ , we introduce an auxiliary classifier $\Psi(\mathbf{z}_f, \mathbf{u})$ which is a 2-layer MLP that takes $\mathbf{z}_f$ and the peptide embedding $\mathbf{u}$ as input and predicts the probability of positive binding label $q_{\Psi}(y \mid \mathbf{z}_f, \mathbf{u})$ , $$ \hat {y} = q _ {\Psi} (Y = 1 \mid \mathbf {z} _ {f}, \mathbf {u}) = \Psi (\mathbf {z} _ {f}, \mathbf {u}) = \mathrm {M L P} (\operatorname {c o n c a t} (\mathbf {z} _ {f}, \mathbf {u})). $$ We define the binding prediction loss using binary cross entropy: $$ \mathcal {L} _ {f \_ c l s} (\hat {y}, y) = - y \log \hat {y} - (1 - y) \log (1 - \hat {y}). $$ # 3.3.2 Structural embedding The structural embedding $\mathbf{z}_s$ is encoded by the structural encoder $\Theta_s(\mathbf{x})$ . There is no control on the information contents of $\mathbf{z}_s$ . However, as $\mathbf{z}_s$ is also used for the sequence reconstruction, with the disentanglement of the embedding space, we expect $\mathbf{z}_s$ to contain all the structural information other than the peptide binding-related patterns, which are encoded in $\mathbf{z}_f$ by design. We also attempted to control the information encoded by $\mathbf{z}_s$ using another auxiliary decoder on $\mathbf{z}_s$ , so that $\mathbf{z}_s$ contains as much information as possible (but not all) about the sequence reconstruction. However, this does not lead to any improvement in the performance (results not shown). # 3.3.3 Disentanglement of the embedding space To regularize the embedding space, we introduce a Wasserstein autoencoder regularization term following [37], by minimizing the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between the distribution of the concatenated embeddings $\mathbf{Z} \sim Q_{\mathbf{Z}}$ where $\mathbf{z} = \mathrm{concat}(\mathbf{z}_f, \mathbf{z}_s)$ and an isotropic multivariate Gaussian prior $\mathbf{Z}_0 \sim P_{\mathbf{Z}}$ where $P_{\mathbf{Z}} = \mathcal{N}(0, I_d)$ , $$ \mathcal {L} _ {\text {W a s s}} (\mathbf {Z}) = \operatorname {M M D} \left(P _ {\mathbf {Z}}, Q _ {\mathbf {Z}}\right). \tag {1} $$ The MMD is estimated as follows: given the embeddings $\{\mathbf{z}_1, \mathbf{z}_2, \dots, \mathbf{z}_n\}$ of an input batch of size $n$ , we randomly sample from the Gaussian prior $\{\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_1, \tilde{\mathbf{z}}_2, \dots, \tilde{\mathbf{z}}_n\}$ with the same sample size. We then use the linear time unbiased estimator proposed by [38] to estimate the MMD, $$ \mathrm {M M D} (P _ {\mathbf {Z}}, Q _ {\mathbf {Z}}) = \frac {1}{\lfloor n / 2 \rfloor} \sum_ {i} ^ {\lfloor n / 2 \rfloor} h ((\mathbf {z} _ {2 i - 1}, \tilde {\mathbf {z}} _ {2 i - 1}), (\mathbf {z} _ {2 i}, \tilde {\mathbf {z}} _ {2 i})), $$ where $h((\mathbf{z}_i, \tilde{\mathbf{z}}_i), (\mathbf{z}_j, \tilde{\mathbf{z}}_j)) = k(\mathbf{z}_i, \mathbf{z}_j) + k(\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_i, \tilde{\mathbf{z}}_j) - k(\mathbf{z}_i, \tilde{\mathbf{z}}_j) - k(\mathbf{z}_j, \tilde{\mathbf{z}}_i)$ and $k$ is the kernel function. Here we use a radial basis function (RBF) [39] with $\sigma = 1$ as the kernel. By minimizing this loss, the joint distribution of the embeddings matches $\mathcal{N}(0, I_d)$ . This loss forces the dimensions of the embedding space to be independent, so that $\mathbf{z}_f$ and $\mathbf{z}_s$ does not share information. Also, the Gaussian shape of the latent space facilitates generation tasks [37, 40]. # 3.3.4 Decoder and reconstruction loss The decoder $\Gamma$ takes as input the combination of $\mathbf{z}_f, \mathbf{z}_s$ and $\mathbf{u}$ to generate a sequence $\mathbf{x}'$ , in the form of amino acid probabilities on each position. The reconstruction loss is the mean position-wise binary cross entropy loss between $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{x}'$ : $$ \mathbf {x} ^ {\prime} = \Gamma (\operatorname {c o n c a t} (\mathbf {z} _ {s}, \mathbf {z} _ {f}, \mathbf {u})) $$ $$ \mathcal {L} _ {r e c o n} (\mathbf {x}, \mathbf {x} ^ {\prime}) = \sum_ {i} ^ {l} - \mathbf {x} ^ {(i)} \log (\mathbf {x} ^ {\prime (i)}) - (1 - \mathbf {x} ^ {(i)}) \log (1 - \mathbf {x} ^ {\prime (i)}), $$ where $l$ is the length of the sequence and $x^{(i)}$ is the probability distribution over the amino acids at the $i$ -th position. Combining all these losses, we have the final objective function: $$ \mathcal {L} = \mathcal {L} _ {r e c o n} + \beta_ {1} \mathcal {L} _ {f \_ c l s} + \beta_ {2} \mathcal {L} _ {W a s s}. $$ # 3.3.5 Justification of the method Following [24], we introduce a measurement of disentanglement as follows: $$ D (\mathbf {X}; \mathbf {Z} _ {f}, \mathbf {Z} _ {s} \mid \mathbf {U}) = V I (\mathbf {Z} _ {s}; \mathbf {X} \mid \mathbf {U}) + V I (\mathbf {Z} _ {f}; \mathbf {X} \mid \mathbf {U}) - V I (\mathbf {Z} _ {f}; \mathbf {Z} _ {s} \mid \mathbf {U}), $$ where $VI$ is the variation of information, $VI(\mathbf{X};Y) = H(\mathbf{X}) + H(Y) - 2I(\mathbf{X};Y)$ , which is a measure of independence between two random variables. For simplicity, we omit the condition $\mathbf{U}$ (peptide) in the following parts. This measurement reaches 0 when $\mathbf{Z}_f$ and $\mathbf{Z}_s$ are totally independent, i.e. disentangled. It could further be simplified as: $$ \begin{array}{l} V I (\mathbf {Z} _ {s}; \mathbf {X}) + V I (\mathbf {Z} _ {f}; \mathbf {X}) - V I (\mathbf {Z} _ {f}; \mathbf {Z} _ {s}) \\ = 2 H (\mathbf {X}) + 2 \left[ I \left(\mathbf {Z} _ {f}; \mathbf {Z} _ {s}\right) - I (\mathbf {X}; \mathbf {Z} _ {s}) - I (\mathbf {X}; \mathbf {Z} _ {f}) \right]. \\ \end{array} $$ Note that $H(x)$ is a constant. Also, according to data processing inequality, as $z_{f} \to x \to y$ forms a Markov chain, we have $I(x;z_f) \geq I(y;z_f)$ . Combining the results above, we have the upper bound of the disentanglement objective: $$ I \left(\mathbf {Z} _ {f}; \mathbf {Z} _ {s}\right) - I (\mathbf {X}; \mathbf {Z} _ {s}) - I (\mathbf {X}; \mathbf {Z} _ {f}) \leq I \left(\mathbf {Z} _ {f}; \mathbf {Z} _ {s}\right) - I (\mathbf {X}; \mathbf {Z} _ {s}) - I (Y; \mathbf {Z} _ {f}). \tag {2} $$ Next, we show how our framework could minimize each part of the upper bound in (2): # Maximizing $I(\mathbf{X};\mathbf{Z}_s)$ Similar to [27], we have the following theorem: Theorem 1 Given the encoder $Q_{\theta}(\mathbf{Z}\mid \mathbf{X})$ , decoder $P_{\gamma}(\mathbf{X}\mid \mathbf{Z})$ , prior $P(\mathbf{Z})$ , and the data distribution $P_{D}$ $$ \mathbb {D} _ {K L} (Q (\mathbf {X}) \parallel P (\mathbf {Z})) = \mathbb {E} _ {p _ {D}} [ \mathbb {D} _ {K L} (Q _ {\theta} (\mathbf {Z} \mid \mathbf {X}) \parallel P (\mathbf {Z})) ] - I (\mathbf {X}; \mathbf {Z}), $$ where $\log Q(\mathbf{Z})$ is the marginal distribution of the encoder when $\mathbf{X} \sim P_D$ and $\mathbf{Z} \sim Q_{\theta}(\mathbf{Z} \mid \mathbf{X})$ . Theorem 1 shows that by minimizing the KL divergence between the marginal $Q(\mathbf{Z})$ and the prior $P(\mathbf{Z})$ , we jointly maximize the mutual information between the data $\mathbf{X}$ and the embedding $\mathbf{Z}$ , and minimize the KL divergence between $Q_{\theta}(\mathbf{Z} \mid \mathbf{X})$ and the prior $P(\mathbf{Z})$ . Detailed proof of the theorem can be found in the supplementary materials. This also applies to the two separate parts of $\mathbf{Z}$ , i.e. $\mathbf{Z}_f$ and $\mathbf{Z}_s$ . In practice, because the marginal cannot be measured directly, we minimize the aforementioned kernel MMD (1) instead. As a result, there is no need for additional constraints on the information content of $\mathbf{Z}_s$ because $I(\mathbf{X};\mathbf{Z}_f)$ is automatically maximized by the objective. We also show in the "Ablation analysis" part in the supplementary that supervision on $\mathbf{Z}_s$ does not improve the model performance. # Maximizing $I(Y; \mathbf{Z}_f)$ $I(Y;\mathbf{Z}_f)$ has an upper bound as follows: $$ I (Y; \mathbf {Z} _ {f}) \geq H (Y) + \mathbb {E} _ {p (Y, \mathbf {Z} _ {f})} \log q _ {\Psi} (Y \mid \mathbf {Z} _ {f}, \mathbf {U}), $$ where $q_{\Psi}(Y \mid \mathbf{Z}_f, \mathbf{u})$ is the predicted label probability by the auxiliary binding classifier $\Psi$ . Thus, maximizing the performance of classifier $\Psi$ would maximize $I(Y; \mathbf{Z}_f)$ . # Minimizing $I(\mathbf{Z}_f;\mathbf{Z}_s)$ Minimization of the Wasserstein loss (1) forces the distribution of the embedding space $\mathbf{Z}$ to approach an isotropic multivariate Gaussian prior $P_{\mathbf{Z}} = \mathcal{N}(0, I_d)$ , where all the dimensions are independent. Thus, the dimensions of $\mathbf{Z}$ will be approximately independent, which also approximately minimizes the mutual information between the two parts of the embedding, $\mathbf{Z}_f$ and $\mathbf{Z}_s$ . # 3.4 Parameter selection and model training The schematic of the TCR-dAE model is shown in Fig. 1A. As the two datasets have been shown to be very different from each other [18], we train two separate models on VDJDB and MCPAS respectively. The dimensionality for $\mathbf{z}_f$ and $\mathbf{z}_s$ are 8 and 32, respectively, selected by grid search. For each input sequence $\mathbf{x}$ , a [CLS] token is added at the beginning as the representative of the sequence as a whole, and an [END] token is added to the end. All sequences are padded to the same length (25). The peptide $\mathbf{u}$ is represented as the average BLOSUM50 score [41] for all its amino acids. The model is trained from end to end using the Adam optimizer [42]. Learning rate, number of epochs and weights of the losses are selected based on grid search. More details about the hyperparameters can be found in the supplementary materials. # 3.5 TCR optimization After training the TCR-dAE model, we are then able to perform TCR optimization by manipulating the model embeddings. Given any TCR sequence $\mathbf{x}$ and a specified peptide $u$ , we transform $\mathbf{x}$ into an optimized TCR that could bind to $u$ as follows (Fig. 1B): 1. Feed $\mathbf{x}$ to the encoder and obtain the functional and structural embedding $\{\mathbf{z}_f, \mathbf{z}_s\}$ of the TCR sequence $\mathbf{x}$ from the encoder. 2. Replace the functional embedding with a new positive one $\mathbf{z}_f^{\prime}$ that indicates binding with $u$ (i.e. $\Psi (\mathbf{z}_f^{\prime},\mathbf{u}) > 0.5)$ . 3. Feed the new embeddings $\mathbf{z}_f^{\prime},\mathbf{z}_s$ (combined with peptide $\mathbf{u}$ as the condition) to the decoder to generate the optimized sequence $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}$ . Sequences are generated in an autoregressive manner, in which each generated amino acid is used as the input for predicting the next one. We use three different methods to obtain the positive functional embedding $\mathbf{z}_f^\prime$ for the given peptide: (1) Random: We use the $\mathbf{z}_f$ of a randomly selected TCR from the positive set. (2) Best: We obtain the $\mathbf{z}_f$ 's for all positive pairs, feed them to the $\mathbf{z}_f$ -based functional classifier $\Psi (\mathbf{z}_f,\mathbf{u})$ with the peptide $\mathbf{u}$ , and then choose the $\mathbf{z}_f$ that produces the highest prediction probability. (3) Average: We take the average of $\mathbf{z}_f$ 's of all positive sequences. As a negative control, we also use $\mathbf{z}_f$ randomly sampled from a multivariate normal distribution for the optimization, labelled null as no functional information is introduced, to ensure that $\mathbf{z}_s$ is not sufficient for sequence optimization. # 3.6 Baseline methods We compare our model with two types of methods for the generation of the optimized TCR $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}$ : (1) mutation-based, which iteratively adds random mutations to the template sequence; and (2) generation-based, which generates novel sequences of the pre-determined length range. For both types of methods, the modified/generated sequences are selected by peptide binding scores from the respective pre-trained ERGO. The experiments are performed on each peptide in the dataset independently. # 3.6.1 Mutation-based baselines # Random mutation (rm) The TCR is randomly mutated by one amino acid for 8 times progressively. This process is repeated for 10 runs for each TCR and the resulting one with the highest ERGO prediction score is reported. # Greedy mutation (greedy) For each TCR, 10 randomly mutated sequences are generated, each with one amino acid difference from the original sequence. Among the 10 mutated sequences, we select the one that gives the highest binding prediction with the given peptide as the template for the next run. This process is repeated 8 times. # Genetic algorithm (genetic) Let $M$ be the sample size. For each TCR, 10 randomly mutated sequences are generated, each with one amino acid difference from the original sequence. All mutated sequences along with the original TCRs are then pooled together, and the top $M$ sequences that give highest binding prediction are used as the input for the next run. This process is repeated 8 times. # 3.6.2 Generation-based baselines # Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) TCRs are generated by adding amino acids iteratively, resulting in a search tree. When TCR length reaches 10, the binding score is estimated by ERGO. For each iteration, a random node is selected for the expansion and evaluated by ERGO, and the scores of all its parent nodes are updated accordingly. The tree expansion ends when the length reaches 20. For every generation process, the highest leaf node is added into the output TCR set. # 3.7 Evaluation metrics We use the following metrics to evaluate whether the optimized sequence $\mathbf{x}'$ (1) is a valid TCR sequence and (2) binds to the given peptide: # Relative edit distance For methods that directly modify the given sequence (TCR-dAE, rm, greedy), we calculate the Levenshtein distance between the template and optimized sequence, normalized by the sequence length: $d = \frac{\mathrm{lev}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})}{\max(l(\mathbf{x}),l(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}))}$ . It is not applicable to genetic mutation or MCTS where samples are pooled for every iteration, and the template information is lost in this process. # Validity score The validity score evaluates whether the generated TCR is "valid", i.e. follows similar patterns and has similar sequence backbones as naturally observed TCRs. We use an autoencoder pre-trained on a separate and much larger dataset of TCR sequences from TCRdb [43], which we denote as TCR-AE, to assess the similarity of a generated TCR with known TCRs. If a generated TCR can be accurately reconstructed by TCR-AE and has similar embedding patterns from TCR-AE as known TCRs, we consider it as a valid TCR. - The reconstruction-based score is calculated as $$ r _ {r} (\mathbf {x} ^ {\prime}) = 1 - \operatorname {l e v} (\mathbf {x} ^ {\prime}, \operatorname {T C R - A E} (\mathbf {x} ^ {\prime})) / l (\mathbf {x} ^ {\prime}), $$ where $\operatorname{lev}(\mathbf{x}', \operatorname{TCR-AE}(\mathbf{x}'))$ is the Levenstein distance between the original sequence and the reconstructed sequence, and $l(\mathbf{x}')$ is the length of the reconstructed sequence. Higher $r_r$ means $\mathbf{x}'$ is better reconstructed from TCR-AE and is thus more likely to be a valid TCR sequence. - The density-based score calculates whether the embedding of $\mathbf{x}'$ follows the same distribution as known TCRs. We learn a Gaussian mixture model from the latent embeddings of known TCRs from TCR-AE. The likelihood of the embedding $\mathbf{e}'$ of $\mathbf{x}'$ from TCR-AE falling in the same Gaussian mixture distribution is denoted as $P(\mathbf{e}')$ . The density-based score is calculated as $$ r _ {d} (\mathbf {x} ^ {\prime}) = \exp (1 + \frac {\log P (\mathbf {e} ^ {\prime})}{\tau}), $$ where $\tau = 10$ . Higher $r_d$ means the latent embedding of $\mathbf{x}'$ from TCR-AE is more likely to follow the same distribution as other valid TCR sequences. We show that these two scores can be used to distinguish valid TCRs from other protein sequences or nonsense sequences (Extended data Fig. 1C). We then define the validity score as $r_v = r_r + r_d$ . We use 1.25 as the threshold for valid TCRs, which excludes most of the nonsense sequences. # Binding prediction The optimized sequence $\mathbf{x}'$ and the peptide $\mathbf{u}$ is fed into the pre-trained ERGO classifier and binding probability $r_p = \mathrm{ERGO}(\mathbf{x}',\mathbf{u})$ is calculated. # 4 Results # 4.1 Disentanglement of the embedding space We obtain the $\mathbf{z}_f$ and $\mathbf{z}_s$ embeddings of the training set from the trained model and use t-SNE [44] for visualization. This lays the foundation for the following experiment of generating optimized sequences using modified $\mathbf{z}_f$ 's. # 4.3 Comparison between TCR optimization methods We use peptides with AUROC $>0.8$ by the classifier $\Psi$ . Optimization is performed on each peptide separately. The evaluation metrics for the methods in comparison are listed in Table 4, where the results are averaged across peptides. Valid sequences refer to those with $r_r + r_d \geq 1.25$ . Positive sequences refer to the valid sequences with $r_p > 0.5$ . For TCR-dAE-based hyperparameter settings, we only report the one with the highest performance on the validation set. To rule out the scenario where $\mathbf{z}_f$ embedding collapses to a very limited set of patterns and modifies all sequences into very similar ones, we use the number of unique sequences in the generated set as an evaluation metric for Table 4. The vast majority of the generated valid sequences (ranging from $70\% \sim 100\%$ across the methods in comparison) are unique (Extended Data Table 3). Furthermore, all valid sequences are not observed in the original dataset (data not shown). We find that TCR-dAE-based methods generate significantly more valid sequences and positive sequences compared to other methods and controls. Among them, the highest performance is achieved by best. Also, though avg could land in positions in the embedding space that does not correspond to any observed sequence, it still generates a decent amount of valid and positive sequences. This shows the embedding space is well regularized and structured by the Wasserstein loss. Performance on VDJDB is generally higher for all methods compared to MCPAS. Thus, in the following analysis, we will use dAE-best on VDJDB by default, unless specified. One advantage of TCR-dAE over other methods is the constraint on the sequence backbone via $\mathbf{z}_s$ from the template. Specifically, MCTS could yield high ERGO binding scores, but most sequences are not valid TCRs because there is no control on the direction of sequence generation. Comparatively, all other baselines and TCR-dAE-based methods, which use known TCRs as templates, could produce relatively more valid sequences. greedy and genetic could produce a moderate amount of valid and positive sequences. The results could be improved by more iterations. However, this would significantly increase the running time, and without control on the sequence backbone, more mutations could result in fewer valid sequences. TCR-dAE, on the contrary, do not require additional running time once the model training is done. Also, greedy, genetic and MCTS all require constant calling of ERGO evaluation at every iteration, otherwise the positive binding property would not be guaranteed like in rm, while TCR-dAE could perform well on the binding score despite not explicitly enforced. Thus, TCR-dAE takes much less time compared to the other methods (Extended Data Table 3). Overall, we demonstrate that TCR-dAE could be used to massively produce candidate TCR sequences with high validity and potentially high binding affinity. # 4.4 Evaluation of optimized TCR sequences It has been well-established that CDR3 regions of TCRs have some conservative patterns [45]. For example, the first three amino acids are almost always 'CAS' and the last three usually follow the 'Q[YF]F' pattern. We pick sequences with length of 15 because it is the most numerous length and averaged the attention values for all attention heads and all samples. As a comparison, we also calculated the mutation frequency on the amino acids for the optimized sequences compared to the templates (Fig. 4B, lower panel). By feeding the optimized sequences back to the encoder, we find that the $\mathbf{z}_s$ of the optimized TCRs show high cosine similarity with those of their templates, while the $\mathbf{z}_f$ do not because the sequences are generated using a different $\mathbf{z}_f$ . However, the $\mathbf{z}_f$ of the optimized TCRs are similar to the $\mathbf{z}_f$ used for their generation (Extended Data Fig. S6D). Prediction of the $\Psi$ classifier for the optimized TCRs agree well with their ERGO prediction (4C). This shows that the optimized TCRs preserve the "structural" information from $\mathbf{z}_s$ and incorporates the new "functional" information from the optimized $\mathbf{z}_f$ . We then investigate whether the optimized TCRs have similar sequence patterns with known positive TCRs. The latent embeddings of the positive optimized sequences from TCR-AE (the pre-trained autoencoder used for evaluation, see Materials and Methods) tend to form into distinct clusters which typically reside in close proximity with those of the true positive sequences (Fig. 4D). Note that TCR-AE is trained on a separate dataset, independent of TCR-dAE and unaware of any functional information. Even though it is not possible to separate positives from negatives using the sequence alone, this observation further proves that certain distinct structural patterns related to binding are carried over from the know positive TCRs to the optimized TCRs. For external validation, we perform a rough binding energy estimation for the optimized TCR and the target peptide. As high quality structures are not available for most TCR-pMHC complexes, we use the classic Miyazawa-Jernigan contact energy [46], which is a knowledge-based pairwise energy matrix for amino acid interactions, and assume all amino acids in the CDR3 $\beta$ of the TCR interacts with all amino acids in the peptide for simplicity. We acknowledge that this estimation is less accurate for longer peptides (e.g. FRDYVDRFYKTLRAEQASQE) where all-to-all interaction is much less likely, making the energy estimation less reliable. Fig. 4E shows that the estimated energy of the positive optimized TCRs has a similar distribution as known positive TCRs, and both are significantly lower than known negative TCRs. One of the causes is that some certain introduced amino acids in the optimized sequence could potentially form non-covalent interactions with the amino acids in the peptide, resulting in lower estimated energy. For example, as in Fig. 4F, the introduction of arginine (R) may lead to lower interaction energy with the aspartic acid (D) in the peptide (CTPYDINQM). This demonstrates that the positive patterns carried by $\mathbf{z}_f$ may have learned, without supervision, some biologically relevant information such as the favored binding energy of the TCR-pMHC complex. # 5 Discussion In this work we present TCR-dAE, a disentangled autoencoder-based framework to massively generate candidate TCRs that bind to a given peptide. The disentanglement constraints separate key patterns related to binding ("functional" embedding) from generic structural backbones ("structural" embedding). By modifying the former while keeping the latter, we are able to generate new TCRs with high binding affinity with the target peptide. We then verified the validity of the optimized TCRs by showing that they follow the same basic structural patterns as known TCRs. Our model outperforms baselines both in quality and quantity. Moreover, as the number of known TCRs is much larger than those with experimentally validated binding, we could use the functional embedding as a signature of the potential peptide binding properties for TCRs. To our knowledge, ours is the first work that approaches TCR sequence optimization from a style transfer perspective. In our problem, the goal of sequence modification is to generate sequences that are similar with known TCR sequences and have higher binding prediction scores. Though the model is trained unaware of either objective, it still succeeds in generating sequences that perform well on both metrics. This indicates that despite not explicitly enforced, the functional and structural embeddings could successfully capture and transfer information about the key functional patterns and generic sequence backbones, respectively. Moreover, there have been several attempts that incorporate a differentiable approximation of evaluation metrics into the training of generative models, to explicitly optimize towards those metrics [47, 48] similar to reinforcement learning. Our framework could also benefit from such methods by back-propagating the optimization objectives to the autoencoder. One difficulty in modelling TCR-peptide interaction, and representation learning of biological data in general, is the lack of experimentally validated negative samples. Recent advances in single-cell techniques have enabled massive profiling of T cell-peptide interactions, but the data is usually limited to a very small number of peptides due to the cost of the experiment [16, 49]. Thus, negative samples need to be obtained by randomly shuffling the positive pairs. This gives rise to the concern that it is impossible to determine whether the shuffled pair is a real negative pair, or an unobserved positive pair (i.e. a false negative). Several negative sampling methods have been proposed to only select the "high confidence" negative pairs [50]. We mitigate this problem by only using the shuffled negative sets that could be well separated from the positives by the interaction predictor ERGO. We are aware that our experiment is performed on a subset selected by ERGO. Meanwhile, as the high confidence positive pairs are scarce, we need to up-sample positive pairs and use ERGO prediction to obtain "true negatives" from unobserved pairs. Thus, the limitations of ERGO itself would bias the results. As can be seen from MCTS results in Table 4, ERGO could predict high scores for totally invalid TCR sequences. This shows current databases and predictive methods are not sufficient to provide a full picture of the TCR-peptide interaction landscape. Incorporating more prior knowledge such as structure and binding energy into the modelling would increase the quality of the generation. Also, the original datasets are highly imbalanced across peptides. As a result, our analysis is restricted to a small set of peptides with a sufficient amount of reliable samples. Because the variability of peptides in the training set is limited, we are not able to directly model the interaction mechanisms between peptides and TCRs using more complex network architectures, thus limiting the generalizability. It is likely that the model learns one distinct set of patterns in the TCR for each peptide, instead of true interactions between the amino acids in the TCR and peptide, so that it cannot model an unseen peptide. A similar phenomenon is observed in [12]. With more high-throughput experimental data accumulated, we will be able to construct more comprehensive models with better generalizability. Nevertheless, our method could still generate large quantities of high quality candidate optimized TCRs for further investigation and more detailed physical modeling. We believe our framework can be further extended to a broader set of protein sequences with more functional terms to consider. A naive approach would be to modify the $\mathbf{z}_f$ -based auxiliary classifier $\Psi(\mathbf{z}_f)$ to predict the function in question. It would then be possible to generate optimized protein sequences with the desired function. # References [1] Gorentla, B.K., Zhong, X.-P.: T cell receptor signal transduction in t lymphocytes.
